questions.model_answer:
a) Entamoeba histolytica. Trophozoite with a single nucleus bearing a small central karyosome and fine, evenly distributed peripheral chromatin; presence of ingested erythrocytes (erythrophagocytosis) is characteristic and distinguishes it from the morphologically identical non-pathogenic E. dispar.
b) Cryptosporidium parvum (C. hominis is morphologically identical). Modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) stain shows round oocysts ~4-6 micrometers (fitting the 6-micrometer ruler) that stain bright pink/red against a blue-green background, often with variable staining and internal sporozoites. Size distinguishes it from Cyclospora cayetanensis (8-10 micrometers) and Cystoisospora belli (elongated, ~20-30 micrometers).
c) Giardia duodenalis (lamblia). Pear/teardrop-shaped trophozoite with two nuclei giving the classic "owl's-face" appearance, or an oval four-nucleate cyst.
questions.beyond_mandell: Chapter 271 (p. 3271) names these organisms as intestinal protozoa but gives no diagnostic morphology; species-level microscopic identification is from the organism-specific Mandell chapters and CDC DPDx.

cohort_answer.text: First H&E image: E. histolytica (E. histolytica may be observed with ingested red blood cells/erythrophagocytosis; E. dispar may occasionally show ingested erythrocytes but to a much lesser degree). Modified acid fast (Kinyoun): Cryptosporidium parvum - oocysts rounded, 4.2-5.4 micrometers diameter, sporozoites sometimes visible indicating sporulation; stained bright red against blue-green background. Second H&E image (c): Giardia lamblia.

questions.model_answer:
a) Soil-transmitted helminths: intestinal worms whose eggs or larvae, passed in human feces, require a period of maturation in warm, moist soil to become infective, with transmission by ingestion of embryonated eggs or by larval skin penetration (no intermediate host).
b) (1) Ascaris lumbricoides (large roundworm). (2) Trichuris trichiura (whipworm). (3) Hookworm - Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale.
c) (1) Iron-deficiency anemia (chronic intestinal blood loss, mainly hookworm). (2) Malnutrition with impaired physical growth and cognitive/educational development in children.
d) (1) Mass drug administration (preventive chemotherapy with albendazole or mebendazole to at-risk groups, especially school-age children). (2) Improved water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) plus health/hygiene education.
e) Loffler syndrome - transient eosinophilic pneumonitis from transpulmonary larval migration (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides), often with asymptomatic peripheral eosinophilia in returning travelers/migrants.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the diagnostic table (species list) is in the read slice (p. 3435); the definition, public-health burden, MDA/WASH control, and Loffler syndrome rest on the Mandell ch. 285 body text and WHO soil-transmitted helminthiasis guidance, not this slice.

cohort_answer.text: Definition: eggs or larvae mature on soil before becoming infective (soil-transmitted helminths, strictly depending on soil environment for a critical developmental stage of life cycle). Most common: Roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides); Whipworm (Trichuris trichiura); Hookworms (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale). Other than Strongy: Ascaris lumbricoides; Trichuris trichiura; Necator americanus; Ancylostoma duodenale. Public health concerns: Iron deficiency anemia (worms feed on host tissues/blood, hookworms cause chronic intestinal blood loss); Malnutrition (increased malabsorption, loss of appetite, roundworms compete for vitamin A); Diarrhea (particularly T. trichiura); Bowel prolapse; Dermatitis; Eosinophilia. Control strategies: Mass drug administration; Improving sanitation; Public knowledge/risk mitigation; Health and hygiene education. Syndrome in developed countries: Asymptomatic eosinophilia; Loeffler's syndrome (eosinophilic pneumonitis - transpulmonary passage of helminth larvae from Ascaris, hookworms, Strongyloides stercoralis; syndrome of transient pulmonary radiographic opacities and peripheral blood eosinophilia; mostly in travelers with first exposure); Strongyloides hyperinfection.
